common_name: Wichita Mountains Goldenrod (Compact Native Prairie Goldenrod)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Wichita Mountains was selected from an Oklahoma wild population for a compact, well-branched habit and heavy fall bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Wichita Mountains goldenrod, selected from a wild population in Oklahoma's Wichita Mountains, forms a compact, well-branched clump topped with dense, bright golden-yellow flower plumes in fall, more restrained and garden-friendly than many taller, more aggressively spreading goldenrod species. It is an outstanding late-season nectar source for native bees, butterflies, and other pollinators at a time when few other perennials are still blooming, and its insect-pollinated, heavy pollen does not become airborne, so it does not cause hay fever despite the common misconception. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in lean, dry soils where richer perennials often struggle, and needs only an occasional division every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Little Lemon Goldenrod (Dwarf Pale Yellow Compact Goldenrod)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Little Lemon is one of the most compact goldenrod cultivars available, staying under a foot tall and well suited to small beds and containers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Little Lemon is a true dwarf goldenrod, forming a tidy, dense mound under a foot tall topped with soft pale-yellow flower clusters in late summer and fall, a gentler color and much smaller scale than most goldenrod species, making it practical for the front of a border, a rock garden, or a container. It draws the same excellent late-season pollinator traffic as larger goldenrods, providing nectar for native bees and butterflies when few other plants are still flowering, and its heavy, insect-carried pollen does not cause hay fever. It is drought-tolerant once established and needs minimal care beyond an occasional division to maintain vigor.

common_name: Vibrant Dome Aster (Compact Magenta-Pink New England Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Vibrant Dome is a sibling selection to Purple Dome, sharing the same compact, mounded, no-staking-needed habit but in magenta-pink.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Vibrant Dome forms a tidy, dense, dome-shaped mound of vivid magenta-pink daisy flowers with golden centers in fall, sharing the same compact, no-staking-needed habit as its sibling selection Purple Dome but in a brighter, warmer pink tone. Like other New England asters it is an exceptional late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies during their fall migration as well as native bees and other pollinators. It performs best with consistent moisture through the summer growing season, and dividing the clump every few years in spring keeps it vigorous and maintains its compact, floriferous form.
